overview: This bill, the DPA Modernization Act, renews and overhauls the Defense Production Act of 1950, a law that lets the federal government prioritize contracts and use loans, purchases and other financial support to make sure U.S. industry can produce what national defense and emergencies require. It extends most of the law's powers through 2031 and reorganizes its sections. The bill makes the Treasury Secretary the manager of the Defense Production Act Fund, raises the cap on the fund's balance from $750 million to $2 billion, and requires each agency using these powers to submit an annual strategy and spending plan. It limits government control over civilian distribution of goods to one year unless the President reports to Congress, lets the President waive regulations to speed purchases and permitting for critical minerals and technologies, bars denying support based on energy source, and makes companies at least 20 percent owned by the President, Vice President or certain officials and their close relatives ineligible for assistance. It also creates a National Defense Executive Reserve of private experts who can be called into temporary federal service in emergencies, adds the Agriculture Secretary to reviews of certain foreign purchases of farmland by buyers from China, North Korea, Russia or Iran, and orders several studies. As of April 15, 2026, a House committee had approved it and it was placed on the House calendar.
for: Supporters say the update gives the government clearer planning, stronger oversight and faster tools to secure supplies of critical minerals, technology and defense goods, while adding conflict-of-interest limits and farmland protections.
against: Critics say the bill expands the fund's size and lets the President waive regulations and permitting rules, which could weaken environmental and other safeguards and concentrate power in the executive branch.
